$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and the given matrix $B,$ we have

$$
{e}^{B}={e}^{PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $3$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)={e}^{x}.$ So, we get

$$
{e}^{J}=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 1-3\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{B} & =P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & -2{e}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3} & -4{e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & -{e}^{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dc2ff6f6-b56f-5924-a7f7-5f180522f2b8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$
{e}^{B}={e}^{PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1}.

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{e}^{J}=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}].

$$
{e}^{B}={e}^{PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({e}^{J})\cdot {P}^{-1}.

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{e}^{J}=[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & {e}^{3} \\ 0 & {e}^{3}\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |"] ["question-7819c8fe-793f-5300-ba05-a00d3d72cc5c" :question/worked-solution "Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$

$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{([\begin{aligned}{J}_{1}(3) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{3}(0)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(3),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =3.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\ .\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{3}(0),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivatives of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(0)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(0) & {f}^{′}(0) & \frac{{f}^{″}(0)}{2} \\ 0 & f(0) & {f}^{′}(0) \\ 0 & 0 & f(0)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{0} & {e}^{0} & \frac{{e}^{0}}{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{0} & {e}^{0} \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{0}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{({J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{3}(0))} & ={e}^{({J}_{1}(3))}\,⊕\,{e}^{({J}_{3}(0))} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Given a square matrix $A$ and a scalar function $f$ with Maclaurin series

$$
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k,
$$

we can define $f(A)$ by replacing $x$ with $A,$ with addition and multiplication performed in the matrix sense:

$$
f(A) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k A^k
$$

For example, recall that the Maclaurin series of $f(x) = e^x$ is

$$
e^x = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{x^k}{k!}.
$$

Then, for a square matrix $A,$ we define the matrix exponential as

$$
e^A = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \dfrac{1}{k!}A^k.
$$

In the next slide, we'll see how to apply matrix functions to square matrices." :tutorial/id #uuid "c3451824-f52b-539c-b16f-3819d3ea37df" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10688 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "215d5365-8c77-5734-bfe7-0ac93d99aa62" :step/math-academy-id 231906 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158092}} {:db/id 17592186158092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158433 :tutorial/content "Suppose $D$ is a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}\end{aligned}]
$$

For a scalar function $f$ with a Maclaurin series expansion, $f(D)$ is the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $f(\lambda_1), \ldots, f(\lambda_n){:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}f({\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & f({\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{aligned}]
$$

For example, given the matrix
$[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$
and the function $f(x) = e^x,$ we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}f(2) & 0 \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}]
$$

This rule works because raising a diagonal matrix to a power is equivalent to raising each diagonal entry to the same power.

Indeed, if
$\displaystyle
f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k$
is the Maclaurin series of $f,$ then, by the definition of $f(D),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(D) & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{D}^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}\end{aligned}]}^{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\lambda }_{n}^{k}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & {\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\sum }_{k=0}^{\infty }{c}_{k}{\lambda }_{n}^{k}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}f({\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & f({\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da162714-f641-5ded-aec8-6f24c0d5cbb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10689 :tutorial/title "Function of a Diagonal Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "c8b4e298-ed67-50ea-bb52-8968e4cd58bf" :step/math-academy-id 231907 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158093}} {:db/id 17592186158093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157268 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157036 :question/id #uuid "5cba0e13-0b34-568b-8a69-eac3fced6338" :question/math-academy-id "e-16515"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "343f8efc-fdef-51dc-ad3f-fad1ab37bc88" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050446} {:db/id 17592186050812}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157695} {:db/id 17592186157699} {:db/id 17592186292544} {:db/id 17592186292545} {:db/id 17592186292546} {:db/id 17592186292552}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Diagonal Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "91d86e1a-5d29-5149-9978-86770afc6de0" :step/math-academy-id 231908 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158094}} {:db/id 17592186158094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158434 :tutorial/content "Suppose $J_n(\lambda)$ is an $n\times n$ Jordan block where the main diagonal entries are all $\lambda{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 1 & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda  & 1 & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & \lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

For a scalar function $f$ analytic at $\lambda$ (i.e., has a Taylor series expansion at $\lambda$), $f(J_n(\lambda))$ is the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{''}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}]
$$

To demonstrate, let's find $f(J_3(2))$ for $f(x) = \ln x.$

Since $J_3(2)$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, we will need the first $3-1=2$ derivatives of $f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}x \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{''}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

![](images/43/439d1a1c3c2c315510fd293e8bb8e1467e149222025359a0e0d899270eb07e12.svg)

Now that we can compute the value of a function of a Jordan block, we can also find the value of a function of a Jordan matrix.

The matrix [math]f(J_n(\lambda))[/math] for [math]n=2,3,[/math] and [math]4[/math] are as follows.

* For [math]2\times 2[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_2(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

* For [math]3\times 3[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_3(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

* For [math]4\times 4[/math] Jordan blocks, we have
\[
f(J_4(\lambda)) =
\begin{bmatrix}
	f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) & \dfrac16f'''(\lambda) \\
	0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac12f''(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\
	0 & 0 & 0 & f(\lambda)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "7972371e-9205-5e74-b277-6dfcab332f9b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10691 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan Block"} :step/id #uuid "deee50a7-b19c-5fb9-80a5-a024ec3943c0" :step/math-academy-id 231911 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158424}} {:db/id 17592186158095 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157269 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157037 :question/id #uuid "f2d8972a-4337-5608-9c82-6fb5e74d22c7" :question/math-academy-id "e-16516"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8ce12d6f-8d1c-52f3-992f-534b9d91dda9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048640}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157696} {:db/id 17592186157700} {:db/id 17592186292547} {:db/id 17592186292553} {:db/id 17592186292554} {:db/id 17592186363586} {:db/id 17592186363595} {:db/id 17592186377004}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Block"} :step/id #uuid "c9bdde30-6bf2-5ffc-93a3-92c41bf6792d" :step/math-academy-id 231912 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158096}} {:db/id 17592186158096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157270 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157039 :question/id #uuid "2bd13883-8376-54f1-9985-83b95f1062a5" :question/math-academy-id "e-16522"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "87883002-67eb-5111-b15a-c5941bb33f9b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157697} {:db/id 17592186157698} {:db/id 17592186292562} {:db/id 17592186292563} {:db/id 17592186292564} {:db/id 17592186363654} {:db/id 17592186363665} {:db/id 17592186377013} {:db/id 17592186377024}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "f4444ff2-15d1-524f-952e-a3223b79ead3" :step/math-academy-id 231915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158097}} {:db/id 17592186158097 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158435 :tutorial/content "Suppose $A$ and $S$ are matrices, where $S$ is invertible.
For a scalar function $f$ with a Maclaurin series expansion, we have
